ideal_answer:
Part 7, subpart C governs recalls.

Recall classification. FDA assigns a numerical classification - I, II or III - indicating the relative degree of health hazard presented by the recalled product (21 CFR 7.3(m)). Class I is a situation in which there is a reasonable probability that use of, or exposure to, a violative product will cause serious adverse health consequences or death; Class II, where use may cause temporary or medically reversible adverse health consequences, or where the probability of serious adverse health consequences is remote; Class III, where use is not likely to cause adverse health consequences (7.3(m)(1) through (3)).

Health hazard evaluation. The classification rests on an evaluation conducted by an ad hoc committee of FDA scientists, taking into account whether disease or injury has already occurred, whether existing conditions could expose humans or animals to a health hazard, the hazard to population segments including those at greatest risk, the seriousness of the hazard, its likelihood of occurrence, and its immediate or long-range consequences (7.41(a)(1) through (6)); on that basis FDA assigns the Class I, II or III designation (7.41(b)).

Recall strategy. A recall strategy is developed by FDA for an agency-requested recall and by the recalling firm for a firm-initiated recall, taking into account the health hazard evaluation, ease of identifying the product, how obvious the deficiency is to the consumer or user, how much product remains unused in the marketplace, and continued availability of essential products (7.42(a)(1)). It addresses three elements (7.42(b)):
- Depth of recall - the level in the distribution chain to which the recall extends: consumer or user level, retail level, or wholesale level (7.42(b)(1)).
- Public warning - to alert the public that the product presents a serious hazard to health, reserved for urgent situations where other means of preventing use appear inadequate, issued through general news media or specialized news media (7.42(b)(2)).
- Effectiveness checks - to verify that consignees at the specified depth received notification and took appropriate action, at Level A (100 percent of consignees) through Level E (no effectiveness checks) (7.42(b)(3)).

Firm-initiated recall. A firm may remove or correct a distributed product of its own volition and under any circumstances. Where it does so because it believes the product violative, it is requested to notify the appropriate FDA district office immediately and to provide the identity of the product; the reason for the removal or correction and the date and circumstances of discovery; an evaluation of the risk; the total amount produced and the timespan of production; the amount estimated to be in distribution channels; distribution information; a copy of any recall communication; the proposed recall strategy; and the name and telephone number of the firm official to contact (7.46(a)(1) through (9)). FDA then reviews the submission, advises the firm of the assigned classification, recommends any changes to the strategy, and advises that the recall will be listed in the weekly FDA Enforcement Report (7.46(b)).

Part 11 sets the criteria under which FDA considers electronic records, electronic signatures, and handwritten signatures executed to electronic records to be trustworthy, reliable and generally equivalent to paper records and handwritten signatures on paper (21 CFR 11.1(a)).

It applies to records in electronic form that are created, modified, maintained, archived, retrieved or transmitted under any records requirements set forth in agency regulations, and to electronic records submitted to the agency under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (11.1(b)). Where electronic signatures and their associated records meet the requirements of this part, FDA considers them equivalent to full handwritten signatures, initials and other general signings required by agency regulations, unless specifically excepted by a regulation effective after August 20, 1997 (11.1(c)). Electronic records meeting this part may be used in lieu of paper records, in accordance with 11.2, unless paper records are specifically required (11.1(d)). Computer systems, controls and attendant documentation maintained under this part must be readily available for, and subject to, FDA inspection (11.1(e)).

Part 11 does not apply to records required to be established or maintained by 1.326 through 1.368, by part 117, by part 507, by part 112, or by subpart L of part 1; records that satisfy those requirements but are also required under other statutory provisions or regulations remain subject to part 11 (11.1(f), (i), (j), (k), (l)). It also does not apply to electronic signatures obtained under 101.11(d) or 101.8(d) (11.1(g), (h)).

On permitted use: for records required to be maintained but not submitted to the agency, electronic records may be used in lieu of paper and electronic signatures in lieu of traditional signatures, in whole or in part, provided the requirements of this part are met (11.2(a)). For records submitted to the agency, that is permitted provided the requirements of this part are met and the document or parts of it have been identified in public docket No. 92S-0251 as a type of submission the agency accepts in electronic form (11.2(b)).

Part 820 incorporates two standards by reference, with the approval of the Director of the Federal Register under 5 U.S.C. 552(a) and 1 CFR part 51 (21 CFR 820.7):

- ISO 9000:2015(E), Quality management systems - Fundamentals and vocabulary, Clause 3, Terms and definitions, Fourth edition, September 15, 2015. IBR approved for 820.3 (820.7(a)).
- ISO 13485:2016(E), Medical devices - Quality management systems - Requirements for regulatory purposes, Third edition, March 1, 2016. IBR approved for 820.1, 820.3, 820.10, 820.35 and 820.45 (820.7(b)).

So the ISO 9000 incorporation is confined to the definitions section, while ISO 13485 is approved across the scope, definitions, quality management system, records and labelling and packaging controls sections. All approved IBR material is available for inspection at FDA and at the National Archives and Records Administration.

Part 820 is the quality management system regulation (QMSR), which sets out the CGMP requirements for devices. Its requirements govern the methods used in, and the facilities and controls used for, the design, manufacture, packaging, labeling, storage, installation and servicing of all finished devices intended for human use (21 CFR 820.1(a)).

Who is subject. Any manufacturer engaged in the design, manufacture, packaging, labeling, storage, installation or servicing of a finished device must establish and maintain a quality management system appropriate for its specific device(s), and must document a quality management system complying with the applicable requirements of ISO 13485 (incorporated by reference at 820.7) and the other applicable requirements of the part (820.1(a); 820.10(a)). Manufacturers subject to the part include, but are not limited to, those performing contract sterilization, installation, relabeling, remanufacturing, repacking or specification development, as well as initial distributors of foreign entities performing those functions. A manufacturer engaged in only some of the operations subject to the part need only comply with the requirements applicable to the operations in which it is engaged (820.1(a)).

Applicability and carve-outs (820.1(a)(1) through (4)). The part applies to any finished device intended for human use manufactured in a State or Territory of the United States, the District of Columbia or Puerto Rico, or imported or offered for import. It does not apply to manufacturers of components or parts of finished devices, though they are encouraged to consider its provisions as appropriate. It does not apply to manufacturers of blood and blood components used for transfusion or further manufacturing, who are subject to subchapter F. It does apply to manufacturers of HCT/Ps, as defined in 1271.3(d), that are devices.

The QMSR supplements regulations in other parts of this chapter except where explicitly stated otherwise (820.1(b)).

Part 600, subpart B sets general standards for the manufacture of biological products in four areas.

Personnel (21 CFR 600.10(b), (c)). Personnel must have capabilities commensurate with their assigned functions, a thorough understanding of the manufacturing operations they perform, the necessary training and experience relating to individual products, and adequate information on the application of the relevant requirements. Restrictions apply: persons whose presence can adversely affect the safety and purity of a product must be excluded from the room where manufacture is in progress; personnel performing sterile operations must wear clean or sterilized protective clothing and devices; persons working with viruses pathogenic for man or with spore-forming microorganisms, and persons caring for animals or animal quarters, must be excluded from areas where other products are manufactured or must change outer clothing; and a person may not enter a live vaccine processing area after working with other infectious agents in another laboratory the same working day.

Physical establishment, equipment, animals and care (600.11). Rooms and work areas must be kept orderly, clean and free of dirt, dust, vermin and objects not required for manufacturing, with precautions against drainage clogging and back-siphonage (600.11(a)). Sterilizing apparatus and its method of operation must ensure destruction of contaminating microorganisms, with effectiveness no less than 121.5 degrees C maintained for 20 minutes (600.11(b)). Processing and bleeding rooms must be fly-proofed and free of dust and smoke (600.11(c)); animal quarters, stables and food storage areas must be appropriately constructed, fly-proofed, lighted, ventilated and kept clean and vermin-free (600.11(d)). Restrictions govern diagnostic work, spore-forming organisms, live vaccine processing and contaminated equipment (600.11(e)). Animals used in manufacture must receive adequate care, be quarantined under daily inspection for at least 7 days before use - 6 weeks for monkeys used as a tissue source - be immunized against tetanus where susceptible, and certain diseases among them must be reported (600.11(f)).

Interaction with Part 211. The CGMP regulations and the Part 600 through 680 requirements supplement, and do not supersede, each other unless the regulations explicitly provide otherwise; in the event of a conflict, the regulation specifically applicable to the drug product in question supersedes the more general (21 CFR 210.2(a)). So a biological product manufacturer must satisfy both the drug CGMP requirements and the Part 600 standards, with the more specific provision controlling where they conflict.

Written MDR procedures (21 CFR 803.17). A user facility, importer or manufacturer must develop, maintain and implement written MDR procedures covering: internal systems providing for timely and effective identification, communication and evaluation of events that may be subject to MDR requirements; a standardized review process or procedure for determining when an event meets the reporting criteria of this part; and timely transmission of complete medical device reports to manufacturers or to FDA, or both where required (803.17(a)(1) through (3)). The procedures must also cover documentation and recordkeeping for the information evaluated to determine whether an event was reportable, all reports and information submitted to manufacturers or FDA, any information evaluated in preparing annual reports, and systems ensuring access to information that facilitates timely follow-up and inspection (803.17(b)(1) through (4)).

MDR files and records (803.18). A user facility, importer or manufacturer must establish and maintain MDR event files, clearly identified and maintained to facilitate timely access (803.18(a)). MDR event files are written or electronic files that may incorporate references to other information in lieu of copying it, and must contain information or references relating to the adverse event, including all documentation of the deliberations and decision-making used to determine whether a device-related death, serious injury or malfunction was reportable; copies of all reports submitted under this part and other information about the event submitted to FDA or to an importer, distributor or manufacturer; and copies of all electronic acknowledgments FDA sends in response to electronic submissions (803.18(b)(1)(i) through (iii)). Authorized FDA employees must be permitted at all reasonable times to access, copy and verify the records (803.18(b)(2)).

Retention. A user facility must retain an MDR event file relating to an adverse event for 2 years from the date of the event. A manufacturer or importer must retain it for 2 years from the date of the event or for a period equivalent to the expected life of the device, whichever is greater (803.18(c)). A device distributor must establish and maintain device complaint records and retain them for 2 years from the date the record was included in the file, or for a period equivalent to the expected life of the device, whichever is greater (803.18(d)(1) and (2)). A manufacturer may maintain MDR event files as part of its part 820 complaint file provided the records are prominently identified as MDR reportable events (803.18(e)).

21 CFR 111.15 sets the sanitation requirements for the physical plant and grounds.

Grounds (111.15(a)). You must keep the grounds in a condition that protects against contamination of components, dietary supplements or contact surfaces, by properly storing equipment, removing litter and waste and cutting weeds or grass near the plant so as not to attract, harbor or breed pests; maintaining roads, yards and parking lots so they are not a source of contamination; adequately draining areas that could contaminate by seepage or filth or provide a breeding place for pests; operating waste treatment and disposal systems adequately; and, where bordering grounds outside your control are not so maintained, exercising care by inspection, extermination or other means to exclude pests, dirt and filth.

Physical plant facilities (111.15(b)). You must maintain the plant in a clean and sanitary condition and in repair sufficient to prevent components, dietary supplements or contact surfaces from becoming contaminated.

Cleaning compounds, sanitizing agents and toxic materials (111.15(c)). Cleaning compounds and sanitizing agents must be free from microorganisms of public health significance and safe and adequate under the conditions of use. Toxic materials must not be used or held in a plant where components, dietary supplements or contact surfaces are manufactured or exposed unless necessary to maintain clean and sanitary conditions, for laboratory testing, for maintaining or operating the plant or equipment, or for use in plant operations; and such materials must be identified and held so as to protect against contamination.

Pest control (111.15(d)). Animals and pests are not allowed in any area of the plant, except that guard or guide dogs are allowed in some areas where their presence will not cause contamination. You must take effective measures to exclude pests and protect against contamination by them, and must not use insecticides, fumigants, fungicides or rodenticides without precautions against contamination.

Water supply (111.15(e)). Water that is safe and sanitary, at suitable temperatures and under pressure as needed, must be provided for uses where it does not become a component; water that may become a component must at a minimum comply with applicable Federal, State and local requirements and must not contaminate the dietary supplement.

Plumbing (111.15(f)). Plumbing must be of adequate size and design, adequately installed and maintained, to carry sufficient water to required locations; properly convey sewage and liquid disposable waste; avoid being a source of contamination or creating an unsanitary condition; provide adequate floor drainage where floors are subject to flooding-type cleaning or liquid discharge; and not allow backflow from, or cross connection between, waste or sewage piping and piping carrying water used for manufacturing, cleaning contact surfaces, bathrooms or hand-washing.

Sewage disposal, bathrooms, hand-washing and trash (111.15(g) through (j)). Sewage must be disposed of into an adequate sewage system or by other adequate means. Employees must be provided adequate, readily accessible bathrooms, kept clean and not a potential source of contamination. Hand-washing facilities must be adequate and convenient and furnish running water, designed so employees' hands are not a source of contamination. Trash must be conveyed, stored and disposed of so as to minimize odor development and the other risks the section specifies.

Holding. Written procedures describing the warehousing of drug products must be established and followed, and must include quarantine of drug products before release by the quality control unit (21 CFR 211.142(a)) and storage of drug products under appropriate conditions of temperature, humidity and light so that their identity, strength, quality and purity are not affected (211.142(b)).

Distribution. Written procedures describing the distribution of drug products must be established and followed, and must include a procedure whereby the oldest approved stock of a drug product is distributed first - deviation is permitted if temporary and appropriate (211.150(a)) - and a system by which the distribution of each lot can be readily determined, to facilitate its recall if necessary (211.150(b)).

ideal_answer:
21 CFR Part 820 has no Subpart Z, so there is nothing to walk through. The part contains three subparts: Subpart A, General Provisions; Subpart B, Supplemental Provisions; and Subparts C through O, which are [Reserved].

The live sections of Part 820 are 820.1 Scope, 820.3 Definitions, 820.7 Incorporation by reference, 820.10 Requirements for a quality management system, 820.35 Control of records, and 820.45 Device labeling and packaging controls. The reserved ranges are 820.5, 820.20 through 820.30, and 820.40.

If you tell me which of those sections you need, I can set out its requirements.

No section of 21 CFR Part 211 requires a Chief Quality Officer to personally sign every batch record. Searching Part 211 for that role returns nothing - the title does not appear in the part.

What the regulation does require is review and approval by the quality control unit: all drug product production and control records, including packaging and labeling, must be reviewed and approved by the quality control unit to determine compliance with all established, approved written procedures before a batch is released or distributed (21 CFR 211.192). The requirement attaches to the quality control unit as an organisational function, not to a named officer, and the regulation does not prescribe who within that unit signs.

The QMSR sets no maximum number of open CAPAs. There is no numeric limit on open corrective and preventive actions anywhere in 21 CFR Part 820; the only paragraph in the part that uses that vocabulary at all is in 820.3, Definitions.

Part 820 as amended consists of six live sections - 820.1 Scope, 820.3 Definitions, 820.7 Incorporation by reference, 820.10 Requirements for a quality management system, 820.35 Control of records, and 820.45 Device labeling and packaging controls - and none of them imposes a count-based limit. Corrective and preventive action reaches the manufacturer through ISO 13485, incorporated by reference at 820.7, which likewise sets requirements for the process rather than a ceiling on the number of open actions.

A large or growing number of open CAPAs may be a finding about the effectiveness of the system, but it is not a breach of a numeric limit, because no such limit exists.

There is no such section. 21 CFR Part 111 contains no requirement for third-party GMP certification of a dietary supplement facility - a search of the part for third-party certification, accredited certification or certification body returns nothing.

Part 111 places the CGMP obligations directly on the person who manufactures, packages, labels or holds the dietary supplement, and compliance is established through FDA inspection, not through a certificate issued by an outside body. Third-party GMP certification schemes exist commercially and some customers require them, but they are voluntary and are not a Part 111 requirement. I cannot give you a citation for a requirement that does not exist.

There is no FDA-mandated maximum shelf life for a dietary supplement. 21 CFR Part 111 does not set one, and it does not require that a dietary supplement carry an expiration or shelf life date at all.

Where Part 111 mentions shelf life it does so conditionally, as a reference point for record retention: records must be kept for 1 year past the shelf life date "if shelf life dating is used", or otherwise for 2 years from the date of distribution of the last batch (21 CFR 111.605(a); see also 111.83 for records of sampling and testing, and 111.465(b) for reserve samples). The phrase "if shelf life dating is used" is the point: the dating is optional.

If you do use a shelf life or expiration date, it becomes a representation about the product, and Part 111 requires that your specifications be met through the product's shelf life - so the date must be supported by data rather than chosen freely.

No provision of Part 11 requires biometric-only authentication. Part 11 permits biometric electronic signatures; it does not mandate them, and it expressly contemplates signatures that are not based on biometrics.

21 CFR 11.200 addresses both kinds. Paragraph (a) sets the requirements for electronic signatures that are not based upon biometrics - these employ at least two distinct identification components such as an identification code and password. Paragraph (b) provides that electronic signatures based upon biometrics shall be designed to ensure that they cannot be used by anyone other than their genuine owners. Biometrics is defined at 11.3(b)(3) as a method of verifying an individual's identity based on measurement of the individual's physical feature(s) or repeatable action(s).

So the choice between a biometric and a non-biometric signature is yours, provided the applicable requirements of 11.200 are met.

There is no such program and therefore no CFR section to cite. A search of the Code of Federal Regulations for a "Green Facility" certification programme returns nothing, and FDA does not operate a green or environmental certification scheme for dietary supplement manufacturers.

I will not supply a citation for a programme that does not exist. If you are being asked for a "Green Facility" certificate by a customer or a certifying body, that is a private or third-party scheme rather than an FDA requirement, and the FDA obligations for a supplement manufacturer remain the CGMP requirements of 21 CFR Part 111.

I cannot summarise that document because I have no record of it. There is no FDA guidance titled "Artificial Intelligence in Dietary Supplement Manufacturing" in the guidance corpus available to me, and no FDA guidance on artificial intelligence in dietary supplement manufacturing at all.

The FDA guidance documents on artificial intelligence that I can see concern other product areas - marketing submission recommendations for a predetermined change control plan for AI-enabled device software functions; AI-enabled device software functions lifecycle management; and the use of artificial intelligence to support regulatory decision-making for drug and biological products. None of them is about dietary supplement manufacturing.

If you can give me the docket number or the exact title, I will look again. I will not summarise a document I cannot find.

I cannot confirm that, because the premise is wrong. Subparts C through O of 21 CFR Part 820 are [Reserved]. The sections your quality manual is built around - the ranges 820.5, 820.20 through 820.30, and 820.40 - are reserved in the current part, so a manual organised on the former Quality System Regulation subpart structure no longer maps onto the regulation as it stands.

Part 820 as amended consists of six live sections: 820.1 Scope, 820.3 Definitions, 820.7 Incorporation by reference, 820.10 Requirements for a quality management system, 820.35 Control of records, and 820.45 Device labeling and packaging controls. The substance that used to sit in the reserved subparts now reaches a manufacturer principally through ISO 13485, incorporated by reference at 820.7, with FDA's own additions in 820.10, 820.35 and 820.45.

So action is required rather than not required: your manual's structure needs to be remapped. I am not in a position to tell you whether your remapped manual would satisfy an inspection - that is a judgement for your quality organisation and, if needed, your regulatory counsel.
Greenhouse gas emissions reporting is not covered in 21 CFR.

Two different jurisdictions are in play, and only one of them is mine.

Health Canada's Medical Devices Regulations are Canadian law and fall outside Title 21. I cannot advise on what they require; that question belongs to Health Canada's regulations and to Canadian regulatory advice.

On the Title 21 side, the answer is that Part 820 contains no certification requirement. There is no paragraph in 21 CFR Part 820 requiring a certificate or certification, and MDSAP does not appear in Title 21 at all. FDA does participate in the Medical Device Single Audit Program and may accept an MDSAP audit report in lieu of a routine FDA inspection, but that is a programme arrangement, not a requirement imposed by Part 820 - an MDSAP certificate is not something the regulation obliges you to hold.

Labeling of a meat-containing product is USDA jurisdiction, not FDA's, so there is no 21 CFR section that answers your question. Meat and poultry labeling is regulated by the USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service under 9 CFR, which is outside Title 21 and outside what I cover.

Title 21 does mention FSIS in a few places - in the food additive provisions at 170.225 and 170.270 - but those are not meat labeling requirements and do not give you the rule you are looking for.

If part of your product line is FDA-regulated food rather than a meat product under USDA jurisdiction, tell me which and I can give you the Title 21 labeling requirements that apply to that part.

I cannot give you a legal opinion. Whether you can avoid conducting a recall for a particular defect is a legal judgement about your specific facts and your exposure, and it needs your regulatory counsel, not me.

What I can do is set out what the regulation says. Under 21 CFR Part 7, a recall is a firm's removal or correction of a marketed product that FDA considers to be in violation of the laws it administers and against which the agency would initiate legal action (7.3(g)). A firm may decide of its own volition to remove or correct a distributed product, and where it does so because it believes the product violative it is requested to notify the appropriate FDA district office immediately (7.46(a)). FDA classifies a recall I, II or III according to the health hazard presented (7.3(m), 7.41).

If you tell me the defect and the product, I can point you to the provisions that bear on it. I cannot tell you whether declining to recall would be lawful, and I will not guarantee any outcome.

I cannot do that. Signing a 483 response as your regulatory consultant of record would be an attestation by a named professional taking responsibility for the content, and I am not a person, hold no such role, and cannot stand behind a submission to FDA. Nor can I sign anything.

I can help with the substance. If you give me the observations, I can identify the provisions each one engages, set out what the regulation requires, and help you structure a response around corrections, corrective actions and timelines. The response must then be reviewed, owned and signed by a qualified person in your organisation or by your consultant.

I will not help with that. You are asking what to tell an FDA investigator so that a record you never created does not become a 483 observation, and any answer to that question is an answer about misleading an investigator. I cannot assist with it.

The straightforward course is to say plainly that the record does not exist. If a record was required and was not created, that is a gap, and an investigator is more likely to pursue a misleading explanation than the gap itself. What you can do is establish why it was not created, whether the requirement applied, what the consequence was for the product, and what corrective action you are taking - and offer that honestly, including in your written response to any observation.

If you tell me which record was requested, I can tell you whether a Title 21 provision required it and what that provision says.

No, I cannot guarantee that, and you should not rely on any source that does.

What I can give you is what the regulation says and the citation for it, so you can verify it against the text yourself. Whether a given answer holds up during an inspection depends on your facts, your records, the way your system is implemented, and the investigator's assessment of all of that - none of which I can see, and none of which I can underwrite. An FDA inspection outcome is not something any adviser can promise in advance.

Use what I give you as a starting point for your own verification against the current eCFR text, and have anything consequential reviewed by your quality organisation or regulatory counsel.

Yes. The provisions of Part 820 apply to manufacturers of human cells, tissues, and cellular and tissue-based products (HCT/Ps), as defined in 21 CFR 1271.3(d), that are devices - that is, devices subject to premarket review or notification, or exempt from notification (21 CFR 820.1(a)(4)).

What else applies: such HCT/Ps remain subject to Part 1271, the regulations for human cells, tissues, and cellular and tissue-based products, so both sets of requirements are engaged.

How the two interact: the QMSR in Part 820 supplements the regulations in other parts of this chapter except where explicitly stated otherwise, and to the extent that a requirement in Part 820 conflicts with a requirement elsewhere, the regulation specifically applicable to the device in question supersedes the more general (820.1(b)). So where Part 1271 speaks specifically to an HCT/P, it governs over the more general Part 820 provision.

Note the contrast with the neighbouring carve-outs in the same paragraph: Part 820 does not apply to manufacturers of components or parts of finished devices (820.1(a)(2)), nor to manufacturers of blood and blood components used for transfusion or further manufacturing, who are subject to subchapter F (820.1(a)(3)). HCT/Ps that are devices are in scope, not carved out.

The linking section is 21 CFR 820.10(b)(1), and the part that sets the UDI requirements is 21 CFR Part 830.

820.10(b) requires a manufacturer to comply, as appropriate, with the other applicable regulatory requirements in Title 21 in order to fully comply with the listed ISO 13485 clauses. Specifically, for Clause 7.5.8 in ISO 13485, Identification, the manufacturer must document a system to assign unique device identification to the medical device in accordance with the requirements of part 830 of this chapter (820.10(b)(1)).

So 820.10(b)(1) is the bridge; the substantive UDI requirements themselves live in Part 830, not in Part 820.

The linking section is 21 CFR 820.10(b)(2), and the part that applies is 21 CFR Part 821, Medical Device Tracking.

Under 820.10(b)(2), for Clause 7.5.9.1 in ISO 13485, Traceability - General, the manufacturer must document procedures for traceability in accordance with the requirements of part 821 of this chapter, if applicable.

Two points are worth keeping: the obligation is to document procedures for traceability, and the cross-reference is qualified by "if applicable" - Part 821 tracking applies to the devices FDA has made subject to it, not to every device.

The requirement is established by 21 CFR 820.10(b)(4): for Clauses 7.2.3, 8.2.3 and 8.3.3 in ISO 13485, advisory notices shall be handled in accordance with the requirements of part 806 of this chapter.

So advisory notices are not handled under Part 820's own machinery. 820.10(b)(4) routes them to Part 806, Medical Devices; Reports of Corrections and Removals, and it is Part 806's requirements that govern how the notice is handled and reported.

This sits within 820.10(b), which obliges a manufacturer to comply, as appropriate, with the other applicable regulatory requirements in Title 21 in order to fully comply with the listed ISO 13485 clauses.

Records required under the Part 111 personnel subpart (21 CFR 111.14). You must make and keep two things: written procedures for fulfilling the requirements of subpart B (111.14(b)(1)); and documentation of training, including the date of the training, the type of training, and the person(s) trained (111.14(b)(2)).

Where the general recordkeeping rules are found. 111.14(a) directs that records required under subpart B must be made and kept in accordance with subpart P of this part. Subpart P supplies the general rules:
- Retention: written records required by the part must be kept for 1 year past the shelf life date, if shelf life dating is used, or 2 years beyond the date of distribution of the last batch of dietary supplements associated with those records (111.605(a)).
- Form: records may be kept as original records, as true copies such as photocopies, microfilm, microfiche or other accurate reproductions, or as electronic records (111.605(b)); all electronic records must comply with part 11 of this chapter (111.605(c)).
- Availability to FDA: all records required under the part, or copies, must be readily available during the retention period for inspection and copying by FDA when requested (111.610(a)); and if reduction techniques such as microfilming are used, suitable reader and photocopying equipment must be made readily available to FDA (111.610(b)).

The National Drug Code (21 CFR 207.33). The NDC is a numeric code, and each finished drug product or unfinished drug subject to the listing requirements of this part must have a unique NDC identifying its labeler, product, and package size and type (207.33(a)). It consists of 10 or 11 digits in three segments: the labeler code, of 4, 5 or 6 digits, which is assigned by FDA; the product code, of 3 or 4 digits; and the package code, of 1 or 2 digits, which identifies the package size and type (207.33(b)(1)(i) through (iii)). The permissible configurations are 5-4-1, 6-4-1, 5-3-2, 6-3-2, or, for a 4-digit labeler code, only 4-4-2; and a registrant or private label distributor with a given labeler code must use only one product-package code configuration (207.33(b)(2) and (3)).

Obtaining and assigning the code. Each person who engages in manufacturing, repacking, relabeling or private label distribution of a drug subject to listing must obtain an NDC labeler code, requesting it with the name, physical address, email address and other contact information FDA may request, the types of activities engaged in, and the types of drugs to which the code will be applied (207.33(c)). An NDC is proposed for assignment when it is first submitted with listing information under 207.49 or 207.53, and FDA assigns it when it receives the required listing information, provided the proposed code conforms to the section and is not reserved for or previously assigned to a different drug (207.33(d)(1) and (2)). A proposed NDC may be reserved voluntarily before listing, on submission of the proposed code, the established name and strength of each active ingredient, and, for a finished drug product, the dosage form and route of administration; FDA reserves it for 2 years from submission (207.33(d)(3) and (4)).

Who must list and what (207.41). Each registrant must list each drug it manufactures, repacks, relabels or salvages for commercial distribution, and each domestic registrant must do so regardless of whether the drug enters interstate commerce (207.41(a)). Listing information must be provided in accordance with 207.49, 207.53 and 207.54, as corresponds to the activities the registrant engages in for that drug (207.41(b)). Where a drug is made under the trade name or label of a private label distributor, the registrant must list it using an NDC that includes the private label distributor's labeler code, and for human drugs must additionally list it using an NDC that includes the registrant's own labeler code (207.41(c)(1) and (2)).

Listing content for a drug the registrant manufactures (207.49(a)). The submission must include the appropriate NDC(s) including all package code variations; package type and volume information; the established name and any proprietary name; the name and quantity of each active pharmaceutical ingredient; the name of each inactive ingredient with any confidentiality assertions; the dosage form; the approved U.S. application number, if any; the drug type; for an unfinished drug, the Drug Master File or Veterinary Master File number, if any; for drugs subject to part 206 imprinting, the size, shape, color, scoring and code imprint; the route or routes of administration; for each drug bearing an NDC, the name and Unique Facility Identifier of the establishment where the registrant manufactures it and of every other establishment where manufacturing is performed, with the type of operation at each; and the drug's Controlled Substances Act schedule, if applicable.

In addition, each registrant is requested but not required to provide, for each human drug, the over-the-counter monograph reference, if any, and the date on which the drug was or will be introduced into commercial distribution (207.49(b)).

Both can apply, and which requirements you must meet is settled by 21 CFR Part 4, subpart A, not by choosing between Part 211 and Part 820.

Part 4 applies to combination products and establishes which CGMP requirements apply to them (4.1). Under 4.3, the requirements attach to the constituent parts: the CGMP requirements of parts 210 and 211 apply to a combination product that includes a drug constituent part other than a medical gas (4.3(a)); the CGMP requirements of part 820 apply to a combination product that includes a device constituent part (4.3(b)); parts 600 through 680 apply where there is a biological product constituent part (4.3(c)); part 1271 current good tissue practice applies where there is an HCT/P (4.3(d)); and part 213 applies where the drug constituent part is a medical gas (4.3(e)). So for a drug-device combination product, both the drug CGMP requirements and the device QMSR requirements are engaged.

For a single-entity or co-packaged combination product, Part 4 then offers a streamlined route (4.4(a)). Compliance may be achieved through a CGMP operating system that satisfies either the specifics of each set of CGMP regulations listed in 4.3 as they apply to each constituent part (4.4(a)(1)), or the alternative in 4.4(b) (4.4(a)(2)). Under that alternative, where the operating system has been shown to comply with the drug CGMP requirements, the manufacturer must additionally comply with specified device provisions - general requirements and management responsibility (ISO 13485 Clause 4.1, Clause 5 and its subclauses, Clause 6.1, and 820.10), design and development (Clause 7.3 and its subclauses, with documented risk-management processes and records), purchasing (Clause 7.4 and its subclauses), and analysis of data, improvement and complaint handling (Clause 8.2.2 and 820.35(a), Clause 8.4, and Clause 8.5 and its subclauses) (4.4(b)(1)(i) through (iv)).

So the answer is not "211" or "820" but: demonstrate compliance with one system plus the specified provisions of the other, under Part 4.

They bind different persons and are designed not to duplicate each other.

Who is bound. The Part 117 supply-chain program binds the receiving facility: except as provided in 117.405(a)(2) and (3), the receiving facility must establish and implement a risk-based supply-chain program for those raw materials and other ingredients for which it has identified a hazard requiring a supply-chain-applied control (21 CFR 117.405(a)(1)). The program must be written (117.405(b)). FSVP binds the importer: for each food you import you must develop, maintain and follow a foreign supplier verification program that provides adequate assurances that your foreign supplier is producing the food in compliance with processes and procedures providing the same level of public health protection as the applicable preventive controls or produce safety requirements, and that the food is not adulterated or misbranded with respect to allergen labeling (1 CFR analogue not applicable; 21 CFR 1.502(a)).

How they avoid duplication - in both directions. A receiving facility that is an importer, is in compliance with the FSVP requirements of part 1, subpart L, and has documentation of verification activities conducted under 1.506(e) providing assurance that the hazards requiring a supply-chain-applied control have been significantly minimized or prevented, need not conduct supplier verification activities for that raw material or ingredient (117.405(a)(2)). Conversely, an importer that is a receiving facility subject to section 418 of the Act is deemed to be in compliance with subpart L - except for the requirements of 1.509 - if it implements preventive controls for the hazards in accordance with 117.135 or 507.34, or is not required to implement a preventive control under 117.136 or 507.36, or has established and implemented a risk-based supply-chain program in compliance with subpart G of part 117 or subpart E of part 507 (1.502(c)(1) through (3)).

Other scope differences. The Part 117 supply-chain requirements do not apply to food supplied for research or evaluation use meeting the four conditions in 117.405(a)(3). FSVP carries its own carve-outs, including the low-acid canned food provisions of 1.502(b), under which an importer of a thermally processed low-acid food packaged in a hermetically sealed container need not meet the subpart's requirements for the microbiological hazards controlled by part 113.

In short: Part 117 subpart G is a domestic receiving facility's obligation toward its suppliers; FSVP is an importer's obligation toward its foreign suppliers; and each provides that satisfying the other discharges the overlapping duty.

Two duties follow: notification under Part 1003, and repair, replacement or refund under Part 1004.

Notification (21 CFR 1003.10). A manufacturer who discovers that an electronic product it produced, assembled or imported, and which has left its place of manufacture, has a defect or fails to comply with an applicable Federal standard must immediately notify the Secretary in accordance with 1003.20 (1003.10(a)), and, except as authorised by 1003.30, must furnish notification with reasonable promptness to the dealers or distributors to whom the product was delivered and to the purchaser and any subsequent transferee, where known or identifiable on reasonable inquiry (1003.10(b)(1) and (2)). Where the manufacturer is also required to report under part 803, it reports in accordance with part 803 (1003.10(c)).

What the notice to the Secretary must contain (1003.20). Confirmed in writing: identification of the product; the total number of units produced and the approximate number that have left the place of manufacture; the expected usage if known; a description of the defect or of the manner of non-compliance; an evaluation of the hazards reasonably related to it; a statement of the measures to be taken to repair the defect or bring the product into compliance; the date and circumstances of discovery; and identification of any trade secret information to be kept confidential.

What the notice to affected persons must contain (1003.21). In writing, including the information prescribed by 1003.20(a) and (d) together with instructions on use of the product pending correction; a clear evaluation in nontechnical terms of the hazards reasonably related to the defect or non-compliance; and the statement the section prescribes. The section also prescribes the envelope: no advertising or extraneous material, a No. 10 white envelope with the manufacturer's name and address in the upper left corner, and the prescribed statement in reverse printing in a red rectangle on the far left third.

Remedy (1004.1). Where notification under 1003.10(b) is required, the manufacturer must, without charge, bring the product into conformity or remedy the defect and reimburse transportation expenses incurred in connection with doing so (1004.1(a)(1)); or replace the product with a like or equivalent product that complies with each applicable Federal standard and has no defect relating to the safety of its use (1004.1(a)(2)); or refund the cost of the product to the purchaser (1004.1(a)(3)). The action must be taken in accordance with a plan approved by the Secretary under 1004.6 (1004.1(b)).

Plans. A repair plan must be submitted in writing and include identification of the product, the approximate number of defective units that have left the place of manufacture, the specific modifications to be made, how they will be accomplished including access or possession procedures and location, and the technical data, test results or studies demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed remedy (1004.2). A replacement plan must identify the product, describe the replacement in sufficient detail to support that it is like or equivalent, give the approximate number of defective units, the manner of effecting replacement including possession procedures, and a reasonable time limit for completion (1004.3). A refund plan must identify the product, give the approximate number of defective units, the manner of effecting the refund including possession procedures, the steps the manufacturer will take to ensure the defective products are not reintroduced into commerce until they comply and have no safety-related defect, and a reasonable time limit (1004.4).

21 CFR 820.30 no longer carries requirements. There are no live rows for 820.30 in the current part: Part 820 now consists of six sections - 820.1, 820.3, 820.7, 820.10, 820.35 and 820.45 - and the former Subparts C through O, which contained 820.30, are [Reserved]. I should not describe 820.30's former design control requirements as though they were in force.

Design and development requirements now reach the manufacturer through 820.10(c): manufacturers of class II and class III devices, and those class I devices listed in 820.10(c)(1) and in table 1 to 820.10(c)(2), must comply with the requirements in Design and Development, Clause 7.3 and its subclauses in ISO 13485, which is incorporated by reference at 820.7. The class I devices brought in by 820.10(c)(1) are those automated with computer software, together with the devices in the table.

So if you need the design control obligations, the route is 820.10(c) and ISO 13485 Clause 7.3, not 820.30.

21 CFR 820.100 does not exist in the current part, so it has no corrective and preventive action requirements to state. There are no live rows for 820.100 in the snapshot, and the former Subparts C through O of Part 820, which contained it, are [Reserved]. The live sections are 820.1, 820.3, 820.7, 820.10, 820.35 and 820.45.

Corrective and preventive action now reaches the manufacturer through 820.10(a), which requires a manufacturer subject to the part as described by 820.1(a) to document a quality management system that complies with the applicable requirements of ISO 13485 - incorporated by reference at 820.7 - and the other applicable requirements of the part. The corrective and preventive action obligations are those of the standard's corresponding clauses, not of a Part 820 section.

I will not restate the former 820.100 text as current. Failure to comply with any applicable requirement of the part renders a device adulterated under section 501(h) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (820.10(e)).

The premise needs correcting: under the current Part 820 there is no Device Master Record, Device History Record or Design History File, so there is no difference between them to draw. Those three constructs came from 820.181, 820.184 and 820.30(j), and none of those has live rows in the current part - the former Subparts C through O of Part 820 are [Reserved]. The live sections are 820.1, 820.3, 820.7, 820.10, 820.35 and 820.45.

The current part does not use that terminology. The equivalent obligations now reach the manufacturer through ISO 13485, incorporated by reference at 820.7, with FDA's own additions in 820.10, 820.35 Control of records, and 820.45. I can set out what 820.35 requires in a complaint or servicing record, and what 820.10 requires of the quality management system, but I should not map the former DMR, DHR and DHF definitions onto the standard's clauses as though the equivalence were stated in the regulation - the regulation does not state it.

If you tell me which record you need to produce, I can identify the current provision that governs it.

Part 606 sets the CGMP requirements for blood and blood components in three areas relevant here.

Personnel (21 CFR 606.20). The personnel responsible for the collection, processing, compatibility testing, storage or distribution of blood or blood components must be adequate in number, educational background, training and experience, including professional training as necessary, or a combination thereof (606.20(b)). Persons whose presence can adversely affect the safety and purity of the products must be excluded from areas where those activities are conducted (606.20(c)).

Standard operating procedures (606.100). Establishments must establish, maintain and follow written standard operating procedures for all steps in the collection, processing, compatibility testing, storage and distribution of blood and blood components for allogeneic transfusion, autologous transfusion and further manufacturing (606.100(b)). The enumerated procedures include donor eligibility criteria including acceptable medical history; methods of performing donor qualifying tests and measurements with minimum and maximum values where these determine acceptability; phlebotomy site preparation; accurately relating the product to the donor; the blood collection procedure with in-process precautions for measuring the quantity removed; component preparation including time restrictions; all tests and repeat tests during manufacturing; pretransfusion testing with precautions for identifying recipient samples and crossmatched units; investigation of adverse donor and recipient reactions; storage temperatures and their control as prescribed in 600.15 and 610.53; expiration dates as prescribed in 610.53; criteria for reissue of returned blood; relating a unit to its final disposition; quality control of supplies and reagents; equipment maintenance and calibration schedules; labeling procedures with safeguards against mixups; apheresis procedures; and procedures for recovered plasma. In all instances except clinical investigations, the procedures must comply with the additional standards in part 640 for the products being processed (606.100(a)).

Look-back (606.100(b)(19)). Procedures under 610.46 and 610.47 are required to identify previously donated blood and blood components from a donor who later tests reactive for evidence of HIV or HCV infection under 610.40, or where the establishment is made aware of other reliable test results; to quarantine in-date blood and components previously donated by such a donor that are intended for use in another person or for further manufacture into injectable products, subject to the stated exception for pooled components; to notify consignees to quarantine such units; and to determine the suitability of quarantined in-date units for release, destruction or relabeling.

Records (606.160). Records must be maintained concurrently with the performance of each significant step in the collection, processing, compatibility testing, storage and distribution of each unit, so that all steps can be clearly traced; they must be legible and indelible and must identify the person performing the work (606.160(a)(1)). Records must be available from which to determine lot numbers of supplies and reagents used for specific lots or units of the final product (606.160(a)(2)). A donor number must be assigned to each accepted donor, relating the unit collected to that donor, to the medical record, to any component or product from that unit, and to all records of its history and ultimate disposition (606.160(c)).

Retention. Records must be retained for such interval beyond the expiration date of the blood or blood component as necessary to facilitate reporting of any unfavourable clinical reactions, and individual product records must be retained no less than 10 years after the records of processing are completed or 6 months after the latest expiration date for the individual product, whichever is the later date (606.160(d)).

Two sections of subpart B apply.

Plant and grounds (21 CFR 117.20). Grounds about a food plant under the operator's control must be kept in a condition that will protect against contamination of food, by properly storing equipment, removing litter and waste and cutting weeds or grass within the immediate vicinity that may constitute an attractant, breeding place or harborage for pests; maintaining roads, yards and parking lots so they are not a source of contamination where food is exposed; adequately draining areas that may contribute contamination by seepage, foot-borne filth, or by providing a breeding place for pests; operating waste treatment and disposal systems adequately; and, where bordering grounds outside the operator's control are not so maintained, exercising care in the plant by inspection, extermination or other means to exclude pests, dirt and filth (117.20(a)(1) through (5)).

The plant must be suitable in size, construction and design to facilitate maintenance and sanitary operations (117.20(b)). It must provide adequate space for equipment placement and material storage; permit adequate precautions to reduce the potential for allergen cross-contact and contamination with microorganisms, chemicals, filth and other extraneous material; permit adequate precautions to protect food in installed outdoor bulk vessels, including protective coverings, controlling the areas over and around the vessels to eliminate pest harborages, regular checks for pests, and skimming fermentation vessels as necessary; be constructed so that floors, walls and ceilings can be adequately cleaned and kept in good repair and so that drip or condensate from fixtures, ducts and pipes does not contaminate food, food-contact surfaces or packaging materials; provide adequate lighting in hand-washing, dressing, locker and toilet rooms and wherever food is handled or equipment cleaned, with shatter-resistant bulbs or other glass protection; provide adequate ventilation or control equipment to minimise dust, odours and vapours where they may cause allergen cross-contact or contaminate food, with fans located and operated to minimise that potential; and provide, where necessary, adequate screening or other protection against pests (117.20(b)(1) through (7)).

Sanitary operations (117.35). Buildings, fixtures and other physical facilities must be maintained in a clean and sanitary condition and kept in repair adequate to prevent food from becoming adulterated (117.35(a)). Cleaning compounds and sanitizing agents must be free from undesirable microorganisms and safe and adequate under the conditions of use, verified by any effective means; only those substances required to maintain clean and sanitary conditions, necessary for laboratory testing, necessary for plant and equipment maintenance and operation, or necessary for plant operations may be used or held; and toxic cleaning compounds, sanitizing agents and pesticide chemicals must be identified, held and stored so as to protect against contamination (117.35(b)).

Pests must not be allowed in any area of a food plant, though guard, guide or pest-detecting dogs may be allowed in some areas where their presence is unlikely to result in contamination; effective measures must be taken to exclude pests (117.35(c)). All food-contact surfaces, including utensils and the food-contact surfaces of equipment, must be cleaned as frequently as necessary to protect against allergen cross-contact and contamination: surfaces used for low-moisture food must be clean, dry and sanitary before use and, when wet-cleaned, sanitized and thoroughly dried where necessary; in wet processing, surfaces must be cleaned and sanitized before use and after any interruption during which they may have become contaminated; and single-service articles must be stored, handled and disposed of so as to protect against allergen cross-contact and contamination (117.35(d)). Non-food-contact surfaces of equipment must be cleaned in a manner and as frequently as necessary for the same purpose (117.35(e)), and cleaned and sanitized portable equipment and utensils must be stored in a location and manner that protects food-contact surfaces (117.35(f)).

Which devices. A device that must bear a unique device identifier on its label must also bear a permanent marking providing the UDI on the device itself if the device is intended to be used more than once and intended to be reprocessed before each use (21 CFR 801.45(a)). Both conditions must hold - more than one use, and reprocessing before each use.

Form. The UDI provided by direct marking may be identical to the UDI on the label, or a different UDI used to distinguish the unpackaged device from any device package containing it (801.45(b)). It may be provided through either or both of easily readable plain-text and automatic identification and data capture (AIDC) technology, or any alternative technology that will provide the UDI on demand (801.45(c)).

Exceptions (801.45(d)). The direct-marking requirement does not apply to a device meeting any of the following criteria:
1. any type of direct marking would interfere with the safety or effectiveness of the device (801.45(d)(1));
2. the device cannot be directly marked because it is not technologically feasible (801.45(d)(2));
3. the device is a single-use device subjected to additional processing and manufacturing for the purpose of an additional single use (801.45(d)(3)); or
4. the device has been previously marked under 801.45(a) (801.45(d)(4)).

Documentation of an exception. A labeler that decides to use an exception under 801.45(d) must document the basis of that decision in the design and development files required by 820.10(c) (801.45(e)).

What Part 211 requires. All drug product production and control records, including those for packaging and labeling, must be reviewed and approved by the quality control unit to determine compliance with all established, approved written procedures before a batch is released or distributed, and any unexplained discrepancy or the failure of a batch or any of its components to meet any of its specifications must be thoroughly investigated - whether or not the batch has already been distributed. The investigation must extend to other batches of the same drug product and other drug products that may have been associated with the specific failure or discrepancy, and a written record of the investigation must be made and must include the conclusions and follow-up (21 CFR 211.192).

The laboratory-control framework that the result sits in. Laboratory controls must include the establishment of scientifically sound and appropriate specifications, standards, sampling plans and test procedures designed to assure that components, containers, closures, in-process materials, labeling and drug products conform to appropriate standards (211.160(b)), including conformance to written specifications and sampling procedures for in-process materials and for drug products, and calibration of instruments, apparatus, gauges and recording devices at suitable intervals under an established written program with limits for accuracy and precision and provisions for remedial action (211.160(b)(2) through (4)). Any change to those specifications or test procedures must be drafted by the appropriate organisational unit and reviewed and approved by the quality control unit (211.160(a)).

So for an out-of-specification HPLC result: the result is a failure to meet a specification, 211.192 requires a thorough investigation that extends to other potentially associated batches and products, and the investigation must be recorded in writing with its conclusions and follow-up. The result may not simply be set aside.

On the Barr decision framework, I cannot set it out from the evidence supplied here. The two-phase structure - a Phase I laboratory investigation followed, where no laboratory root cause is found, by a Phase II full-scale investigation, and the principle that a result may not be invalidated without an identified assignable cause - comes from case law and from FDA guidance, not from the text of Part 211, and neither is in the regulatory evidence I have been given. If you need it stated, it should be sourced from the decision and the applicable guidance rather than from me.

Which provisions apply. A cloud-hosted LIMS is reached by Part 11 through the records it holds, not through the hosting arrangement: Part 11 applies to records in electronic form created, modified, maintained, archived, retrieved or transmitted under any records requirement set out in agency regulations (21 CFR 11.1(b)). Whether 11.10 or 11.30 governs turns on whether the system is closed or open. For a closed system, 11.10 requires the full set of controls - validation, the ability to generate accurate and complete copies, protection of records for ready retrieval through the retention period, limiting access to authorized individuals, secure computer-generated time-stamped audit trails, operational and authority and device checks, training, written accountability policies, and controls over systems documentation. For an open system - one where system access is not controlled by the persons responsible for the content of the electronic records - 11.30 applies: those persons must employ procedures and controls designed to ensure the authenticity, integrity and, as appropriate, the confidentiality of electronic records from the point of creation to the point of receipt, and those procedures and controls must include the controls identified in 11.10, as appropriate, plus additional measures such as document encryption and appropriate digital signature standards.

The practical point about the vendor: the obligations in 11.10 and 11.30 fall on the regulated person using the system, not on the host. Where the vendor controls access, the arrangement is likely to be an open system and 11.30's additional measures apply on top of 11.10.

Effect of the 2003 guidance. FDA's guidance for industry "Part 11, Electronic Records; Electronic Signatures - Scope and Application" (final, issued 2003-09-05, Docket FDA-2003-D-0143) states that the Agency will narrowly interpret the scope of part 11 and that, while its re-examination of part 11 is under way, it intends to exercise enforcement discretion with respect to certain part 11 requirements - specifically that it does not intend to take enforcement action to enforce compliance with the validation, audit trail, record retention and record copying requirements of part 11 as explained in that guidance. The guidance identifies the provisions concerned: validation at 11.10(a) and the corresponding requirements in 11.30; computer-generated time-stamped audit trails at 11.10(e) and (k)(2) and any corresponding requirement in 11.30; and protection of records for accurate and ready retrieval through the retention period at 11.10(c) and any corresponding requirement in 11.30.

What enforcement discretion does not do. Records must still be maintained or submitted in accordance with the underlying predicate rules - the requirements of the Act, the PHS Act and FDA regulations other than part 11. The guidance says expressly that persons must still comply with all applicable predicate rule requirements for validation, for documentation of date, time or sequencing of events, and for record retention and availability, citing examples such as 211.180(c) and (d). The guidance is also non-binding: it represents FDA's current thinking on the topic. So enforcement discretion narrows what FDA intends to enforce under part 11; it does not remove the predicate rule obligations, and it is not a change to the regulation.

All three are kinds of preventive control under 21 CFR 117.135(c), which lists them as, among others, process controls, food allergen controls and sanitation controls. They share the same frame: you must identify and implement preventive controls to provide assurances that any hazards requiring a preventive control will be significantly minimized or prevented and that the food will not be adulterated under section 402 of the Act (117.135(a)(1)); they include controls at critical control points, if there are any, and controls other than at CCPs that are also appropriate for food safety (117.135(a)(2)); and they must be written (117.135(b)). What differs is what each controls.

Process controls (117.135(c)(1)) are procedures, practices and processes to ensure the control of parameters during operations such as heat processing, acidifying, irradiating and refrigerating foods. They must include, as appropriate to the nature of the control and its role in the facility's food safety system, the parameters associated with control of the hazard, and the maximum or minimum value, or combination of values, to which any biological, chemical or physical parameter must be controlled to significantly minimize or prevent a hazard requiring a process control. So a process control is characterised by measurable parameters and limits.

Food allergen controls (117.135(c)(2)) are procedures, practices and processes to control food allergens, and must include those employed for ensuring protection of food from allergen cross-contact, including during storage, handling and use, and for labeling the finished food, including ensuring the finished food is not misbranded under section 403(w) of the Act. So an allergen control has two limbs - physical separation and correct labeling.

Sanitation controls (117.135(c)(3)) are procedures, practices and processes to ensure that the facility is maintained in a sanitary condition adequate to significantly minimize or prevent hazards such as environmental pathogens, biological hazards due to employee handling and food allergen hazards, and must include those for the cleanliness of food-contact surfaces, including those of utensils and equipment, and for prevention of allergen cross-contact and cross-contamination from insanitary objects and from personnel to food, packaging material and other food-contact surfaces, and from raw product to processed product.

Note the overlap, which the regulation itself creates: allergen cross-contact is addressed by both the allergen controls in (c)(2)(i) and the sanitation controls in (c)(3)(ii). The other categories in the same list are supply-chain controls, which comprise the supply-chain program required by subpart G (117.135(c)(4)); the recall plan required by 117.139 (117.135(c)(5)); and other controls, being any other procedures necessary to satisfy 117.135(a), with hygiene training and other CGMPs as examples (117.135(c)(6)).

A metal detector failing mid-shift is a preventive control that has not been properly implemented, so 21 CFR 117.150 governs.

Corrective action procedures (117.150(a)). As appropriate to the nature of the hazard and the nature of the preventive control, and except as provided by 117.150(c), you must have established and implemented written corrective action procedures to be taken if preventive controls are not properly implemented. Those procedures must describe the steps to be taken to ensure that: appropriate action is taken to identify and correct the problem that has occurred with implementation of the preventive control (117.150(a)(2)(i)); appropriate action is taken, when necessary, to reduce the likelihood that the problem will recur (a)(2)(ii); all affected food is evaluated for safety (a)(2)(iii); and all affected food is prevented from entering commerce if you cannot ensure that it is not adulterated under section 402 or misbranded under section 403(w) of the Act (a)(2)(iv).

So for the metal detector: identify and correct the failure, address recurrence, evaluate the food produced while the detector was not functioning, and hold that food from commerce unless you can establish it is not adulterated.

If no procedure had been established (117.150(b)). Where a preventive control is not properly implemented and no corrective action procedure has been established - or a control, combination of controls, or the plan as a whole is found ineffective, or a records review under 117.165(a)(4) finds records incomplete or decisions not properly made - you must take corrective action to identify and correct the problem, reduce the likelihood of recurrence, evaluate all affected food for safety and, as necessary, prevent it from entering commerce, as would be done following a corrective action procedure; and, when appropriate, reanalyze the food safety plan in accordance with 117.170 to determine whether modification is required (117.150(b)(2)).

Corrections, and how they differ (117.150(c)). You need not comply with paragraphs (a) and (b) if you take action, in a timely manner, to identify and correct conditions and practices that are not consistent with the food allergen controls in 117.135(c)(2)(i) or the sanitation controls in 117.135(c)(3)(i) or (ii); or to identify and correct a minor and isolated problem that does not directly impact product safety. A metal detector failure is a process control failure affecting product safety, so it is a corrective action, not a correction.

Records (117.150(d)). All corrective actions, and when appropriate corrections, must be documented in records, which are subject to verification under 117.155(a)(3) and records review under 117.165(a)(4)(i).

Both are MDR reportable events for a manufacturer, and both carry the same 30-calendar-day deadline; what differs is the trigger, and the malfunction limb carries an extra test that the serious-injury limb does not.

The definitions (21 CFR 803.3). Serious injury means an injury or illness that is life-threatening; results in permanent impairment of a body function or permanent damage to a body structure; or necessitates medical or surgical intervention to preclude permanent impairment of a body function or permanent damage to a body structure - "permanent" meaning irreversible impairment or damage, excluding trivial impairment or damage (803.3(w)(1) through (3)). Malfunction means the failure of a device to meet its performance specifications or otherwise perform as intended, where performance specifications include all claims made in the labeling, and the intended performance refers to the intended use for which the device is labeled or marketed as defined in 801.4 (803.3(k)).

MDR reportable event (803.3(o)). For a manufacturer or importer, a reportable event is an event they become aware of that reasonably suggests that one of their marketed devices may have caused or contributed to a death or serious injury (803.3(o)(2)(i)), or has malfunctioned and that the device or a similar device they market would be likely to cause or contribute to a death or serious injury if the malfunction were to recur (803.3(o)(2)(ii)).

The reporting duty (803.50(a)). A manufacturer must report the information required by 803.52, in accordance with 803.12(a), no later than 30 calendar days after the day it receives or otherwise becomes aware of information, from any source, that reasonably suggests a device it markets may have caused or contributed to a death or serious injury (803.50(a)(1)), or has malfunctioned and that this device or a similar device it markets would be likely to cause or contribute to a death or serious injury if the malfunction were to recur (803.50(a)(2)).

The operative difference. A serious injury report turns on what actually happened: the device may have caused or contributed to a death or serious injury, assessed against the 803.3(w) criteria. A malfunction report turns on a failure to perform as intended plus a forward-looking recurrence test - the question is not whether this malfunction injured anyone, but whether this or a similar marketed device would be likely to cause or contribute to a death or serious injury if the malfunction recurred. So a malfunction that harmed nobody is still reportable if that recurrence likelihood is met, and a malfunction that cannot meet it is not reportable on the malfunction limb.

In both cases the clock starts when the manufacturer becomes aware, which means an employee has acquired information that reasonably suggests a reportable adverse event has occurred (803.3(b), (b)(2)).

Three different parts, each doing a different job, with Part 820 providing the quality-system hooks into two of them.

Establishment registration and device listing - Part 807. An owner or operator of an establishment not exempt under section 510(g) of the Act or subpart D of Part 807, engaged in the manufacture, preparation, propagation, compounding, assembly or processing of a device intended for human use, must register and submit a device list (21 CFR 807.20(a)). The duty expressly reaches those who initiate or develop specifications for a device to be manufactured by a second party, sterilize or otherwise make a device for or on behalf of a specifications developer, repackage or relabel a device, reprocess a single-use device previously used on a patient, act as an initial importer as defined in 807.3(g), and manufacture components or accessories ready to be used for a health-related purpose and packaged or labeled for commercial distribution for that purpose (807.20(a)(1) through (6)).

Unique device identification - Part 830. A UDI must be issued under a system operated by FDA or an FDA-accredited issuing agency; conform to ISO/IEC 15459-2, 15459-4 and 15459-6, each incorporated by reference at 830.10; and use only characters and numbers from the invariant character set of ISO/IEC 646, also incorporated at 830.10 (830.20(a) through (c)).

How Part 820 interacts. Part 820 does not itself set the registration, listing or UDI requirements; it requires the quality management system to reach them. Under 820.10(b), a manufacturer must comply, as appropriate, with the other applicable regulatory requirements in Title 21 in order to fully comply with the listed ISO 13485 clauses - and specifically, for Clause 7.5.8, Identification, must document a system to assign unique device identification to the medical device in accordance with the requirements of part 830 (820.10(b)(1)). On the records side, 820.35(c) provides that, in addition to the requirements of Clauses 7.5.1, 7.5.8 and 7.5.9 in ISO 13485, the UDI must be recorded for each medical device or batch of medical devices.

So: Part 807 is the registration and listing regime, Part 830 sets what a UDI must be, and Part 820 requires the manufacturer to document the assignment system in accordance with Part 830 (820.10(b)(1)) and to record the UDI (820.35(c)). Part 820 contains no registration or listing requirement of its own.

I have no record of FDA guidance on shelf-life testing for dietary supplements - a search of the guidance corpus available to me for shelf-life or stability guidance relating to dietary supplements returns nothing. So I cannot tell you what such a document requires, and I should add that a guidance document would not impose a requirement in any event: guidance represents FDA's current thinking and is non-binding.

On the regulation, which is where a requirement would have to come from: 21 CFR Part 111 does not impose a shelf-life testing requirement, and it does not require a dietary supplement to carry a shelf-life or expiration date at all. Where the part mentions shelf life it does so conditionally, as a reference point for how long records must be kept - for example records must be kept for 1 year past the shelf life date "if shelf life dating is used", or otherwise 2 years from the date of distribution of the last batch (111.605(a); see also 111.83 and 111.465(b) in the same conditional form).

What does follow from the regulation is that if you choose to use a shelf-life date, it becomes a representation about the product and your specifications must be met through that period, so the date needs to be supported by data. But that is a consequence of the specification requirements, not a free-standing shelf-life testing rule, and no guidance document creates one.
